newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Gold Banc keeps community touch.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Gold Banc keeps community touch.

text.p: In an era of bank consolidation, with super-regionals gobbling up smaller banks, Leawood, Kansas-based Gold Banc Corp is trying to succeed by focusing on local businesses looking for a personal touch.
"We hear about a lot of customers who are unhappy with changes taking place" through consolidation, Gold Banc chief executive Michael Gullion said in an interview.
That consolidation included the acquisition of Missouri-based Boatmen's Bancshares by NationsBank Corp earlier this year.
Gold Banc is having some success attracting customers that are not comfortable at larger banks, offering, among other things, decentralized loan approval by local bank officers.
Gold Banc's loans outstanding grew to $213 million at the March 31 first quarter from $203 million in the fourth quarter. Gullion said the pace picked up in the second quarter.
"Both the deposit growth and the loan growth that took place in the first quarter of 1997...the second quarter (growth) will be substantially above that," Gullion said.
Gold Banc, headquartered in the affluent suburban-Kansas City area of Johnson County, focuses on loans to owner-operated businesses.
Aside from relying on economic growth in Johnson County and picking up customers disgruntled with larger banks, Gold Banc, which went public in November, is also looking to grow through acquisitions.
"Ideally, we'd like to see two to three acquisitions a year," Gullion said.

Gold Banc, with $310 million in assets at the end of the first quarter, targets banks with $50-150 million in assets, though it would consider smaller and larger acquisition targets. These banks are typically too small to be of interest to a larger bank holding company.
Other criteria include being headquartered in a county seat in Kansas or Missouri, having number one or number two market share and strong asset quality.
What Gold Banc brings to these acquisitions is enhanced technology and pooling of some resources. What it gets is a relatively inexpensive source of funds to loan.

"In my opinion, the limit to their strategy is having access to those rural Kansas deposits," said Wayne Bopp, analyst at Robert W. Baird & Co Inc. Bopp, who has a buy rating on the stock, said for the time being there are enough banks in rural Kansas to satisfy Gold Banc's acquisition appetite.
Gullion said the bank is planning to have telephone banking, bill-paying service and personal computer banking by the third quarter, and possibly Internet banking in 1998.
Focusing more on personal service and relationship banking can be expensive, but Gold Banc is working on cutting costs.

Its efficiency ratio, a measure of the cost of raising each dollar of revenue for a bank, came down to a still lofty 66 percent in the first quarter from just under 80 percent in the second quarter of 1996.
The bank's goal is to bring that below 60 percent, possibly by the end of the year.
But that is still above the 50 percent range of some larger banks.

"At some point in time you have to decide whether you're a processing institution or a service institution," Gullion said. "We believe that our customer base is willing to pay more for perceived value."
Baird's Bopp agreed, noting that most of Gold Banc's loan customers are entrepreneurs who don't want to spend a long time trying to get a loan from a large bank, only to be turned down.
"They'll pay a little bit more just to have consistant access to capital," Bopp said.
((Chicago newsdesk, 312-408-8787))
